title: The only question you need to ask about education technology.
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Meyer answers a teacher's request for an edtech evaluation checklist with a single test: what does the product do with wrong answers? His point is that students spend most of their math time producing under-formed thinking, and software that only says not quite wastes it. He gives a concrete example of a student who reverses x and y coordinates and is given the same generic message as for any nonsense input. In his Desmos Sand Dollar Search example, the reversed answer instead makes a crab appear where the student typed, creating productive cognitive dissonance. He extends the standard to curriculum and teachers: the best technology makes room for varied right and wrong ideas and helps the class find value in them. He discloses that he works at Desmos.
points: Meyer proposes one evaluation question for any edtech product: does it waste wrong answers or put them to work?
Every wrong answer is a mix of correct and incorrect thinking, so effective teaching scrutinizes it rather than dashing past it.
Feedback that mirrors the student's input, like the crab popping up at (4,3), creates cognitive dissonance without telling the student they are wrong.
The same standard applies to a curriculum or a teacher, who can interpret student answers literally to show the need for precise mathematics.
He discloses that he works at Desmos, which does well by this standard.
quotes: If I have one minute with your product, if you lure me over to your booth at a conference with candy, if someone sends me a link to your website, I'll do the same thing every time:
I'm not saying we should protect students from knowing when they're wrong. I'm saying that every wrong answer is a resource and we shouldn't waste it.

Every wrong answer is the product of thinking that is correct and incorrect, formal and informal, developed and developing. The work of teaching is to help students understand and develop their thinking.

When the student presses "Check," the software tells them "Not quite," which is the same message it sends if the student types in anything—the number 420, the entire shooting script of Bee Movie, a cry for help—anything.
The student experiences a moment of cognitive dissonance. "The crab did not pop up where I thought it would." Their mind works to resolve it.
The best technology makes something easy out of something hard, which is why I'll always give a second look to edtech that takes a student's wrong answers and puts them to work.
